title: Does Checking for Attention Work?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles weighs in on a running debate between David Didau, Christian Moore Anderson, and Pritesh Raichura over whether high-frequency "checking for attention" questioning during teacher explanations actually helps students learn. Rather than siding fully with either camp, Salles offers a resolution: checking for attention is performative and can actively interfere with learning, because a student answering correctly after every sentence proves only that they tracked one fragment, not that they grasped how the parts of an explanation cohere into a whole. His key distinction is between attention as a proxy and understanding as the actual goal, arguing that focusing instruction on the proxy (repeating back fragments) can crowd out the deeper processing needed to build a coherent mental model of the full explanation. Salles proposes concrete alternatives designed to check understanding rather than attention: pre-teaching five key words students must use in their own written reconstruction, sentence-by-sentence cloze exercises, and pre-testing with questions before the explanation to activate prior knowledge and exploit the pretesting effect. He is careful to note these techniques still make attention more likely as a side effect, through priming, partner scaffolding, and public cold-calling, but insists the instructional target must remain understanding, not the performative appearance of listening.
points: Reframes a three-way blog debate (Didau, Anderson, Raichura) by arguing attention-checking is performative and treats a proxy for learning (repeating back a fragment) as if it were the goal itself.

Explains the specific mechanism of harm: students focused on surviving the next cold-call question attend to isolated fragments of an explanation rather than to how its parts cohere into a whole understanding.

Distinguishes checking for attention from checking for understanding, arguing the latter correctly targets "a lack of learning" directly rather than an intermediate proxy that can be satisfied without real comprehension.

Offers concrete, replicable alternatives — five-word cued reconstructions, sentence-by-sentence cloze exercises, and pre-explanation pretesting to activate prior knowledge — that check understanding while still increasing attention as a side effect.

Concedes that his recommended techniques still make attention more likely through priming and public cold-call, but insists the instructional target and the felt experience for students must be understanding, not surveillance.
quotes: High-frequency questions a teacher fires out at students, pretty much after every sentence of an explanation. The questions are designed for 100% of students to be able to answer successfully, provided they were paying attention.

We're confronted with a room full of children in which some are attentive, some pretending, some drifting, some lost, some trying hard but failing to track. Our problem is practical and immediate: how do we know whether every students is with me right now?

If I have attended to every part of your explanation, and to every question after every part of your explanation, will I have a better understanding of the whole explanation? That is not my experience of students in the classroom.

What I am very unlikely to be doing is paying attention to how the different parts of the explanation stick together. Too much has got in the way. I might never fail to repeat what my teacher has said. But the whole explanation is much less likely to cohere.
Your goal is not attention, your goal is learning. Attention is a proxy for learning and can actually get in the way of learning if you focus on the proxy itself.
But, I am not checking for attention. I am checking for understanding. My students, your students, will feel that difference.
